node.label: Pat Hudson
node.date_label: The Genesis of Industrial Capital (1986) · The Industrial Revolution (1992) · History by Numbers (2000) · Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution, with Maxine Berg (2023)
node.description: In The Genesis of Industrial Capital (1986), Pat Hudson explained industrial development in West Riding wool textiles through agrarian structures, landholding and varied routes from domestic to factory production. Her 1990 working paper with Maxine Berg, Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution, argued that regional transformation and women’s and children’s work expose changes obscured by national growth measures. With Berg, she later argued that slave-based Atlantic markets helped generate industrial skills and innovation, challenging Joel Mokyr’s supply-side explanation in 2021. Their Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023) connected slavery to production, consumption, finance and inequality. In 2025 Priya Satia criticized the book’s causal disclaimers as inconsistent with the force of its evidence and challenged its portrayal of earlier scholarship.

node.scope_note: Selected passages of the 1990 working paper and 2021 response read. The 1992 journal article was checked for metadata only. The Genesis of Industrial Capital and History by Numbers are represented by publisher summaries; the 2014 chapter by its publisher summary. The 2023 monograph is represented by its authors’ account and a named critic; its body is unread. Underlying datasets and numerical results were not independently checked.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hudson and Maxine Berg coauthored Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The authors introduce their substantive joint monograph. Publication and coauthorship only; no inference of influence between the coauthors. Book body unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Berg, Hudson’s “Slavery, Atlantic trade and skills” (2021) challenges Mokyr’s supply-side skills explanation, arguing that slave-based Atlantic demand better explains industrialisation’s timing and regional concentration.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Joint response read at pp. 260–261 and 275–276. The authors retain a role for skilled artisans. Their objection concerns causal stimulus, timing and geography; Mokyr’s original lecture is unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Atlantic demand challenges a skills-first explanation

proposed_edges.relationship: With Berg, Hudson’s Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution (1990 working paper) questions causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s national demographic aggregates, emphasizing regional and social variation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected working-paper pages 30–33 read, including the acknowledgment of Schofield’s subsequent revision. This supports a qualified methodological criticism, not a rejection of population reconstruction. The preliminary paper is not substituted for the unread 1992 journal body.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Slavery, the slave trade and economic growth” (2014), Hudson re-examines Williams’s account of slavery and British industrialisation through regional and sectoral analysis, as described in the publisher’s chapter summary.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher summary only. It establishes a named reassessment, not agreement with every Williams thesis. Full chapter and Williams’s book unread in this task. Original 2014 distinguished from the later platform date.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reassesses Williams on slavery and industrialisation

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Genesis of Industrial Capital (1986), Hudson connects West Riding domestic industry and factory transition to agrarian structures and changing landholding, according to the publisher’s summary.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter summary read; empirical chapters unread. The claim concerns this regional explanation, not a national test or endorsement of the entire proto-industrialisation thesis.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Berg, Hudson’s Rehabilitating the Industrial Revolution (1990 working paper) makes women’s and children’s work, wage differentials and work discipline central to explaining industrial change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected labour-force section pp. 20–23 read. A substantive intervention on gendered labour, not a claim that Hudson founded gender history. The 1992 journal body is unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women’s and children’s work in industrial change

proposed_edges.relationship: History by Numbers (2000) presents quantitative methods through historical problems and data, explaining their purposes and interpretive pitfalls, according to the publisher’s description.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description and first-edition metadata only. This is a bounded methodological contribution; examples and calculations in the book were not independently read or replicated. No co-credit relationship is proposed from this textbook.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Slavery, Capitalism and the Industrial Revolution (2023), Berg and Hudson argue that slavery shaped British production, consumption, investment and enduring inequalities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Authors’ full account of their book read. Joint attribution retained. No claim that slavery was a sufficient or necessary sole cause; the monograph is unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Slavery and the structures of British capitalism
